title: Small Islands Want Remittances to Fund Climate Defence | Across the Water, Ep. 13
lede: At the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, a group of small island developing states proposed a SIDS Diaspora Resilience Fund, designed with IIED: an islands-owned remittance platform charging senders 3% per transfer, against average market costs of about 5–9%, with 2–2.5 percentage points of each transfer going into a permanent endowment for climate resilience. The goal is eventually about US$3 billion a year. This episode explains the mechanics, the adaptation-finance gap it targets, the Caribbean-first rollout and what still has to happen.
keyPoints: The proposed platform would charge 3% per transfer; after costs, 2–2.5 percentage points would go into an endowment (Reuters, Nov 13, 2026).

Small island states received just over US$2 billion a year in international public adaptation finance in 2021–22, 44% of it debt; they need about US$12 billion a year (Climate Policy Initiative, 2025).
Year one of the rollout: the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Jamaica and Guyana. Base case: a US$2.59 billion endowment by year 10 (Reuters; IIED).
The Dominican Republic received US$11.87 billion in remittances in 2025 (Banco Central RD); Jamaica US$3.12 billion in fiscal 2025/26.
Next: a meeting of development banks and island leaders in January, aiming for progress by COP32 in 2027 (Reuters).
